Article Title: Delhi protest crackdown: 20 FIRs registered, assault on cops among charges
Article Text:
The protest, which called for Kumar's resignation, was met with a massive security deployment and widespread detentions across the national capital

Supreme Court steps in over restrictions

CJP alleges 'open Emergency'

NEW DELHI: Delhi Police has registered 20 FIRs in connection with the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP)-led protest against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, officials told news agency PTI on Sunday.The cases include charges of assaulting police personnel and obstructing public servants from discharging their duties. One FIR registered at Kamla Market police station relates to the alleged assault on students and manhandling of women during the protest. Four men claiming links to the right-wing Hindu Raksha Dal have been arrested in the case, officials said.The protest, which called for Kumar's resignation, was met with a massive security deployment and widespread detentions across the national capital on Saturday. More than 7,000 people, including opposition leaders and activists, were detained as police erected barricades and deployed thousands of personnel to prevent demonstrators from reaching Jantar Mantar. Several incidents of stone-throwing were reported, leaving more than 15 police personnel injured, including Deputy Commissioner of Police (South) Anant Mittal.Amid the fallout, the Supreme Court on Sunday directed authorities to ensure that people gathering peacefully are not illegally detained and that Delhi Metro services operate normally, subject to law and order conditions.The bench of Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana also directed that internet services remain undisturbed and that lawyers and journalists not be obstructed from performing their professional duties.The court issued a notice to the Centre while hearing a plea seeking contempt proceedings over alleged violations of its directions concerning restrictions on metro and train services during the protest. It also ordered authorities to remove a notice board outside the Supreme Court premises announcing the imposition of Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), which restricts assemblies of five or more people.Meanwhile, CJP activists Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka accused the administration of imposing excessive restrictions to suppress what they described as a youth-led movement."The situation across the country right now mirrors an open Emergency. Such repressive conditions have not been witnessed since the dictatorial regime of 1975," Das said, alleging that Delhi had been turned into a "cantonment".He also criticised the closure of metro stations, suspension of train services and shutdown of markets, claiming the restrictions were inconveniencing ordinary citizens and turning public sentiment against the protest.Ranka separately condemned the police's handling of activist Abhijeet Dipke, alleging that personnel showed insensitivity while informing him of his grandmother's death.
Article Summary: Delhi Police has registered 20 FIRs in connection with the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP)-led protest against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. The cases include charges of assaulting police personnel and obstructing public servants from discharging their duties. Four men claiming links to the right- wing Hindu Raksha Dal have been arrested in the case.

Article Title: Watch: CPM MP John Brittas argues with Delhi Police as they attempt to detain him
Article Text:
Brittas said the CJP leaders had been treated worse than hijackers. (PTI)

NEW DELHI: CPM Rajya Sabha MP John Brittas on Sunday got into a heated argument with Delhi Police personnel as they attempted to detain him amid a political row over the detention of Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) chief Abhijeet Dipke and other party leaders.Brittas, along with CPM MP A A Rahim, had criticised the police action against Dipke, Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, who were reportedly detained aboard their flight from Mumbai after it landed at Indira Gandhi International Airport on Saturday.Speaking to reporters in Delhi, Brittas said the CJP leaders had been treated worse than hijackers or people accused of major financial scams.“The central government is doing all this because they are scared. The police could have arrested them once they come out of the airport. They could not have escaped from inside the airport. There was no need to detain them from inside the plane,” he said.Brittas also condemned the action against journalists, alleging that several were detained or prevented from reporting on the protests, PTI reported.He accused Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Union home minister Amit Shah of taking such measures to protect Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.Rahim alleged that several CJP activists and protesters who resisted restrictions on the demonstration at Jantar Mantar or objected to the removal of their phones were “brutally tortured”.Dipke, Ranka and Das were released on Sunday after being produced before the Special Executive Magistrate (SEM) Court at Delhi Cantonment Police Station.Delhi Police said the three were preventively arrested under Sections 126 and 170 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) on October 10 and produced before the court on October 11.The police said the three were released after furnishing a surety bond of Rs 50,000, with a condition to maintain peace and good behaviour for one year.CJP legal affairs head Ratna Singh also confirmed their release, saying it was subject to an undertaking to maintain public order. “Condition - no breach of peace for one year,” she posted on X.Before his release, Dipke had alleged in a video posted on Instagram that Delhi Police personnel entered his flight to detain him and his associates after they landed in Delhi.“So, you can see that Delhi Police is entering the plane to arrest us. They are all entering the plane. We just landed. All the Delhi Police officers are standing in the aisle. They are trying to arrest us from inside the plane. The entire Delhi Police is getting on the plane. This is the fear of Narendra Modi...Not even Indira Gandhi did this during the Emergency. All we wanted to do is a peaceful protest, and they are picking us up from the flight like we are criminals,” Dipke said.The detention of the CJP leaders came amid a major security clampdown in Delhi on Saturday. Delhi Police detained protesters, activists and political leaders at multiple locations, including along routes leading to Jantar Mantar, where the CJP had planned to hold a demonstration.The party and opposition groups have been demanding Kumar’s resignation over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. Delhi Police had denied permission for the gathering, and many protesters were detained before they could reach the proposed venue.More than 7,000 protesters were detained at multiple locations, according to the details provided. Several opposition leaders, including former chief ministers Arvind Kejriwal, Mamata Banerjee, Pinarayi Vijayan and Manik Sarkar, were also detained while attempting to join the protest.
Article Summary: CPM Rajya Sabha MP John Brittas got into a heated argument with Delhi Police personnel as they attempted to detain him. Brittas, along with CPM MP A A Rahim, had criticised the police action against Dipke, Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das. They were reportedly detained aboard their flight from Mumbai after it landed at Indira Gandhi International Airport.

Article Title: Watch: PM Modi inaugurates Rs 4,900 crore Chennai Metro Phase II stretch, rides train with CM Vijay
Article Text:
PM Modi took a ride on the newly inaugurated stretch with CM Joseph Vijay.

Chennai Metro services

: Timings and stations

PM Modi offers prayers

Highway, port and railway projects on agenda

NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Sunday inaugurated the Poonamallee-Vadapalani stretch of Phase II of the Chennai Metro Rail Project, built at a cost of around Rs 4,900 crore.He also took a ride on the newly inaugurated stretch with Tamil Nadu chief minister C Joseph Vijay.PM Modi and Vijay jointly flagged off the new Metro services in the presence of Tamil Nadu Governor Rajendra Vishwanath Arlekar. The Prime Minister also purchased a ticket and briefly interacted with an employee at the ticket counter.The newly inaugurated stretch is part of Corridor 4 of Phase II and covers around 15 km, with 11 elevated Metro stations. The corridor features a unique 3.7-km double-decker structure and advanced signalling systems designed to support driverless operations.The new stretch is expected to reduce daily commuting time and improve connectivity between Chennai’s western suburbs and the city centre.According to Chennai Metro Rail, regular passenger services on the new stretch will begin at 4 pm on Sunday and operate in both directions until 9 pm.From October 12, services will run daily from 7 am to 9 pm.The last train will depart at 9 pm from both terminals: Poonamallee Bypass Metro and Vadapalani Metro on Corridor 4.The 11 stations on the new stretch are Poonamallee Bypass, Poonamallee Bus Stand, Poonamallee Government Hospital, Karayanchavadi, Kumananchavadi, Kattupakkam, Iyappanthangal, Thelliyaragaram, Porur Bypass, Porur Junction and Vadapalani.Earlier, Modi offered prayers at the Sri Jalakanteswara Swamy Temple in Tamil Nadu. He later visited the Sudha Gopalakrishnan Brain Centre at IIT Madras.The Prime Minister is also scheduled to dedicate the centre to the nation. The facility is part of a scientific initiative to map more than 100 human brains into three-dimensional atlases at cellular resolution, covering different stages of life, from the foetal stage to old age.PM Modi will also release C-STROKE, a human ischaemic stroke atlas featuring more than 1,000 annotated microscopic sections from a stroke-affected brain. The atlas is expected to help researchers identify potential new targets for treatment.Later in the day, the Prime Minister is scheduled to attend the golden jubilee celebrations of Jaigopal Garodia Hindu Vidyalaya Matriculation Higher Secondary School.During his visit, Modi will inaugurate and lay the foundation stones for National Highway projects worth around Rs 3,700 crore in Tamil Nadu.The key projects include the 36-km, four-laned Vadugapatti-Therkuvenganallur section of NH-744A, the 30-km, four-laned Madurai Ring Road section of NH-744A, and the four-lane Thiruvarur Bypass on the Nagapattinam-Thanjavur section of NH-83.He will also inaugurate five Amrit Stations at Palani, Vellore Cantonment, Ambasamudram, Paramakkudi and Namakkal.Several port-related projects at Chennai Port, Kamarajar Port and V O Chidambaranar Port are also on the agenda. These projects aim to strengthen maritime infrastructure, expand cargo-handling capacity and improve logistics efficiency.The PM will also lay the foundation stone for a Group II/III Lube Oil Base Stocks (LOBS) project at the existing Manali Refinery of Chennai Petroleum Corporation Limited (CPCL).The project, estimated to cost around Rs 1,620 crore, will have a capacity of 270 thousand metric tonnes per annum. It aims to manufacture Group II/III lube oil base stocks for producing premium-quality lubricants in India.
Article Summary: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Sunday inaugurated the Poonamallee-Vadapalani stretch of Phase II of the Chennai Metro Rail Project. He also took a ride on the newly inaugurated stretch with Tamil Nadu chief minister C Joseph Vijay. PM Modi will also lay the foundation stones for National Highway projects worth around Rs 3,700 crore.

Article Title: ‘It's now or never’: India Youth Congress calls for mass mobilisation in Delhi on October 12 over ‘vote chori’ allegations
Article Text:
Indian Youth Congress has announced a protest on October 12 to defend democracy and the Constitution.

NEW DELHI: Indian Youth Congress has announced a ‘Chalo Delhi’ mobilisation on October 12, urging people to join its campaign to defend the Constitution and democracy amid the Congress-led Opposition’s allegations of electoral irregularities and its demand for accountability from the Election Commission.The announcement comes amid a series of protests by Rahul Gandhi and other INDIA bloc leaders against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.In a series of posts on X, the youth wing used the slogan “It's NOW or NEVER” and accused the BJP of rigging elections with the help of a “compromised Election Commission”. It called on people to stand up peacefully for their voting rights, freedom and constitutional protections.The organisation also invoked Mahatma Gandhi and India's freedom struggle, arguing that the country belongs to its people and not to any political party. The posts repeated the October 12 date and the slogan, “For our Constitution. For our democracy. For each other.”The announcement follows protests by Rahul Gandhi and other Opposition leaders in New Delhi. On October 8, Delhi Police detained Gandhi, Congress leader Priyanka Gandhi Vadra and around 90 other Opposition MPs and workers as they attempted to reach Jantar Mantar for a demonstration against the Election Commission.On October 9, Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge and Rahul Gandhi led an INDIA bloc delegation that submitted a memorandum to President Droupadi Murmu against what the Opposition calls “vote chori”.According to the Congress's official press release, the delegation raised concerns about the electoral process and sought the President's intervention. The meeting was part of the Opposition's broader campaign challenging the Election Commission's handling of electoral rolls and demanding accountability from its leadership.
Article Summary: Indian Youth Congress has announced a ‘Chalo Delhi’ mobilisation on October 12. The announcement comes amid a series of protests by Rahul Gandhi and other INDIA bloc leaders against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. The youth wing accused the BJP of rigging elections with the help of a “compromised Election Commission”

NEW DELHI: A day after police cracked down on the Cockroach Janta Party’s (CJP) proposed protest in Delhi, Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) supremo Arvind Kejriwal turned his fire on Prime Minister Narendra Modi , invoking Hitler to attack the Centre’s handling of the demonstration and warning that the demand for resignation could extend beyond CEC Gyanesh Kumar.In a video shared on X, Kejriwal accused the authorities of mistreating protesters, including young women, lawyers and journalists, during Saturday’s crackdown.Also read: Turn any spot into your own Jantar Mantar, says Arvind Kejriwal “The way Modi ji unleashed a reign of terror yesterday, he crossed all limits and left even Hitler behind. It should not come to a point where, along with Gyanesh Kumar, Modi ji himself is forced to resign this time,” Kejriwal said in a video message.The CJP had called for a mass demonstration at Jantar Mantar, demanding Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation over SIR. However, an extensive security crackdown significantly curtailed the planned protest, with police detaining party leaders and supporters across the national capital.CJP leaders Abhijeet Dipke, Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das were among those detained after arriving at Delhi’s Indira Gandhi International Airport. Police also detained several opposition leaders, including Kejriwal, West Bengal chief minister Mamata Banerjee and Kerala chief minister Pinarayi Vijayan, along with YouTuber Dhruv Rathee.The crackdown resulted in more than 7,000 detentions, triggering allegations of excessive restrictions on peaceful assembly and the treatment of protesters.The Supreme Court has issued notice to the Centre on a contempt plea alleging violation of its earlier directions and called for measures to prevent illegal detention of peaceful protesters and ensure normal transport services.

Article Title: 'Ambani won't go out of business': Elon Musk says Starlink competition would benefit Indians
Article Text:
Musk says Starlink’s entry into India would give consumers more choices

NEW DELHI: SpaceX CEO Elon Musk on Sunday said that competition from Starlink would "benefit Indian consumers" by offering them more choices, arguing that Reliance Industries chairman Mukesh Ambani would not go out of business even if his profits declined.In a post on X, Musk criticised what he described as arguments made by Ambani’s supporters against Starlink’s entry into India, calling them “absurd hypocrisy and hyperbole”.“On the one hand, they say Starlink couldn’t possibly compete with the amazing low prices offered by Ambani’s de facto monopoly in India and then, in the same breath, they essentially claim that Starlink would be too strong of a competitor!” Musk wrote.“The reality is that competition would greatly benefit the average citizen in India by giving them more choices, as it always does. Ambani’s profits will be lower, but he is not going out of business,” he added.Musk also argued that Starlink would have to make its services affordable to attract customers. “And, obviously, if Starlink is too expensive in India, no one will buy it, so SpaceX will need to make pricing affordable,” he said.Musk’s latest remarks come amid a dispute over the delay in Starlink’s commercial rollout in India. On Friday, he took a swipe at Ambani, addressing him as “Prime Minister Ambani” and alleging that he was the “real boss of India”.“Dear Prime Minister Ambani, Please accept my humble apologies for not realizing that you are the real boss of India. Naturally, you would prefer to maintain your monopolistic exploitation of the great people of India, but would you nonetheless consider allowing Starlink to compete?” Musk wrote in an earlier post.He has also alleged that unnamed business groups are trying to obstruct Starlink’s entry to protect their market positions. The government has rejected the allegations, maintaining that the delay is linked to pending regulatory and security requirements.At the India Mobile Congress 2026 in New Delhi, Union communications minister Jyotiraditya Scindia said India would not permit a monopoly in any sector and that three satellite communication operators had received licences: Reliance Jio Satcom, Bharti Airtel-backed Eutelsat OneWeb and Starlink.However, the government has said security clearances remain pending for the licensed operators. The satellite spectrum pricing framework is also being finalised, and commercial services can begin once the prescribed requirements are met.
Article Summary: SpaceX CEO Elon Musk says Starlink's entry into India would give consumers more choices. He argues that Reliance Industries chairman Mukesh Ambani would not go out of business even if his profits declined. Musk also argued that Starlink would have to make its services affordable to attract customers. His latest remarks come amid a dispute over the delay in Starlink’s commercial rollout in India.

Article Title: ‘Blatant attack on press freedom’: Journalists’ bodies condemn detention of journalists at Delhi protest
Article Text:
A protestor being dragged towards a detention bus during Jantar Mantar 2.0 on October 10 in Delhi

Reporters taken to detention centres, equipment seized

‘PIB accreditation cannot determine who can report’

NEW DELHI: Four journalists’ organisations on Saturday expressed concern over the detention of journalists covering protests in Delhi demanding chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation, saying the incident raised serious questions about press freedom.The Press Club of India (PCI), Indian Women’s Press Corps (IWPC), Delhi Union of Journalists (DUJ) and Delhi unit of the Kerala Union of Working Journalists (KUWJ) said journalists were targeted while documenting the police action. In a joint statement, they alleged that reporters carrying valid press identity cards were taken away and that some had their phones and reporting equipment confiscated, news agency PTI reported.The organisations termed the action a “blatant attack on the freedom of press” and demanded the immediate release of all detained journalists.According to the statement, journalists covering Saturday’s protests were put on buses and taken to locations including Chhatrasal Stadium and Chanakyapuri police station, alongside hundreds of protesters detained by the police.The organisations said reporters were filming the detentions when police personnel took them into custody, despite their displaying press cards. They also cited complaints that officers refused to acknowledge their journalistic credentials, with some allegedly remarking, “Everybody claims to be a journalist these days.”The statement further alleged that official reporting phones belonging to some of the detained journalists were taken away.The four bodies also objected to the Delhi Police’s reported insistence that only journalists accredited by the Press Information Bureau (PIB) could cover the protests.“Press freedom in India cannot be conditional on PIB accreditation. A large section of digital and independent media does not have PIB cards, yet they are recognised press under the law,” they said.The organisations said they had flagged the issue in a memorandum to the Delhi Police commissioner earlier in the week. However, they alleged that the concerns and recommendations raised in the representation had not been addressed.They sought an inquiry into the role of senior police officers who allegedly directed the detention of journalists even after being shown their press identification cards. Their demands also included the return of seized equipment, a public apology from Delhi Police and an assurance that reporters would be free to cover demonstrations without interference.They also said the restrictions, coupled with the detention of journalists, undermined the ability of the media to report on public protests and question institutions.“Preventing journalists from doing their job, detaining them without reason, and creating a fortress-like situation in the capital with 22,000 police and paramilitary, closed metro stations and unprecedented internet shutdowns, to stop peaceful questioning of institutions is reminiscent of a fascist state,” the statement said.
Article Summary: Four journalists’ organisations express concern over the detention of journalists covering protests in Delhi. They allege that reporters carrying valid press identity cards were taken away and that some had their phones and reporting equipment confiscated. The organisations termed the action a ‘blatant attack on the freedom of press’ and demanded the immediate release of all detained journalists.

Beyond the five days

“Chill! It’s just periods. You’ll feel better in a couple of days.”But do women really get better in three to five days or are they caught in a recurring loop of exhaustion, mood swings and hormonal shifts that returns month after month from their first period till end.From hormonal fluctuations and ovulation to fatigue, bloating and premenstrual symptoms, the menstrual cycle is a month-long process that extends far beyond the days of bleeding. Yet, what happens inside the body between periods remains poorly understood by many women.For some, menstruation brings severe cramps, exhaustion and an overwhelming need to be left alone. Others struggle with bloating, back pain, irritability or difficulty concentrating at work. And for many, the days leading up to a period can be just as challenging as the bleeding itself.“I feel like somebody is constantly stabbing me with a sword, not even a knife, in my stomach,” says Sasha Singh, describing her experience of menstruation.“Emotionally, I am so annoyed that eye rolls become the only friend that day. The Luteal phase is the worst for me, an indication of days ahead,” she added.For Shivanghi, the physical discomfort comes with an emotional toll.“I feel like I need to punch whoever is talking to me and cry all the time. Physically its like my insides are getting drained and sawed repeatedly. I feel the first day and the day before that are the most painful.”Their experiences highlight how differently women can experience the menstrual cycle, both physically and emotionally. They also raise a larger question: What happens inside the body when there is no bleeding?Menstruation is the shedding of the uterine lining through the vagina when pregnancy has not occurred. The bleeding contains blood and tissue from the lining of the uterus, also called the endometrium.Periods generally last between three and seven days, although the duration and amount of bleeding vary. Menstruation usually begins during puberty, most commonly between the ages of 11 and 14, though it can start earlier or later. It continues through the reproductive years until menopause, which typically occurs between the ages of 45 and 55.The menstrual cycle, however, covers the entire interval from the first day of one period to the first day of the next.A cycle is often described as lasting 28 days, but this is only an average. Many adults have cycles that fall within a range of approximately 21 to 35 days, and cycle length can vary with age and individual circumstances.The cycle is regulated by hormones that coordinate activity between the brain, the ovaries and the uterus. Its four commonly described phases are menstruation, the follicular phase, ovulation and the luteal phase.Importantly, these phases are not four completely separate stages. The follicular phase begins on the first day of menstruation and continues until ovulation, meaning the first two phases overlap.The menstrual cycle begins on the first day of menstrual bleeding. When pregnancy has not occurred, the levels of hormones that support the uterine lining fall, prompting the lining to shed.The uterus contracts to help expel this tissue, which can cause cramps in the lower abdomen and sometimes pain in the lower back. Some women also experience bloating, headaches, fatigue, breast discomfort or changes in mood.According to Priyanka, the first two days can be particularly difficult. “During my period, I usually feel physically tired, bloated and uncomfortable, with severe cramps and lower back pain. Emotionally, I tend to feel more irritable, sensitive and overwhelmed than usual. The most challenging phase for me is the few days leading up to my period the Luteal phase, when PMS symptoms like mood swings, fatigue and bloating are at their peak. The first two days of my period can also be difficult,” she added.Hormone levels, particularly those of oestrogen and progesterone, are relatively low at the beginning of the cycle. But this does not mean that the body's reproductive processes have stopped. As menstruation begins, hormones are already signalling the ovaries to start developing follicles for the next stage.For most women, some discomfort during menstruation can be managed with appropriate measures. However, severe pain that interferes with daily activities should not automatically be dismissed as a normal part of having periods.This phase starts on the first day of menstruation and continues until ovulation.During this time, the pituitary gland releases follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), which stimulates the development of follicles in the ovaries. Each follicle contains an immature egg, and usually one becomes dominant and continues to mature.As the follicle develops, it produces increasing amounts of oestrogen. This hormone helps rebuild and thicken the uterine lining after menstruation.The changes are taking place even after the bleeding stops, although they may not produce obvious symptoms.Some women report feeling more energetic or focused during the days after their period. Others do not notice any clear difference. These experiences can vary from one person to another and even from one cycle to the next.Vijaya notices significant changes in her energy and concentration around her cycle. “Oh yes!! It changes drastically. Energy drops, concentration is hindered. Sleep becomes overpowering, as if body is on energy saver mode.”However, it is important not to assume that every change in energy or mood is caused by menstrual hormones. Sleep, stress, nutrition, underlying health conditions and other factors can also influence how someone feels.The follicular phase illustrates why the menstrual cycle is more than a monthly episode of bleeding. While the body prepares an egg for possible release, the uterine lining is also being rebuilt.As the dominant follicle matures, rising oestrogen levels help trigger a surge in luteinising hormone (LH). This surge causes ovulation, when the ovary releases a mature egg.Ovulation is often described as occurring around day 14 of a 28-day cycle, but its timing varies. It does not necessarily happen on the same day for everyone, or even in every cycle for the same person.After its release, the egg enters the fallopian tube, where it may be fertilised by sperm. The egg usually remains capable of fertilisation for approximately 12 to 24 hours. However, pregnancy can occur from sex in the days leading up to ovulation because sperm can survive in the reproductive tract for several days.Some women notice changes around ovulation, while some experience mild pain on one side of the lower abdomen. Others may notice no obvious physical changes.There is also considerable variation in whether women report changes in mood, energy or sexual desire around this time. These experiences should not be treated as universal signs of ovulation.Understanding ovulation is important not only for those trying to conceive but also for anyone seeking to understand the timing of their cycle. Calendar estimates and period-tracking apps can help identify patterns, but they cannot always predict the exact day of ovulation.After ovulation, the follicle that released the egg transforms into a structure called the corpus luteum. It produces progesterone, along with some oestrogen, to help maintain the uterine lining in preparation for a possible pregnancy.If pregnancy does not occur, the corpus luteum breaks down. Progesterone and oestrogen levels fall, triggering changes that eventually lead to the shedding of the uterine lining and the start of the next period.For some women, the luteal phase brings premenstrual syndrome (PMS), with symptoms such as bloating, breast tenderness, headaches, fatigue, irritability, food cravings and disturbed sleep.The intensity varies, with some experiencing mild discomfort while others struggle with symptoms that affect their work and daily lives. In severe cases, symptoms may indicate premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD), which can cause significant emotional and physical distress.The emotional effects can be difficult to explain. “Getting irritated all the time and crying for no reason. It feels like everyone is being rude and they all hate me,” says Shivanghi.Priyanka also reports increased irritability and anxiety, while Vijaya notices a drop in energy and concentration. Hormonal fluctuations may also coincide with acne, changes in appetite and digestive issues such as bloating, constipation or diarrhoea.Persistent acne, unexplained hair loss, increased facial hair, substantial weight changes or ongoing digestive problems can also be automatically attributed to the menstrual cycle. However, severe or persistent symptoms that interfere with daily life warrant medical assessment.The effects of the menstrual cycle can extend beyond reproductive organs. Changes in oestrogen and progesterone may influence several bodily functions, although the extent of these effects differs between individuals.According to Dr Asha Susawat, senior obstetrician and gynaecologist at Cocoon Hospital, Jaipur, hormonal fluctuations can influence how women feel throughout the cycle.“While the hormonal fluctuations will be much more impactful than just your bleeding pattern, their importance will vary from woman to woman. For some, high levels of oestrogen before ovulation make them feel more energetic. Others will not perceive any significant differences. Following the occurrence of ovulation, the progesterone hormone increases the temperature levels in the body and may affect the sleep pattern. As the woman starts to bleed, some may feel sleepy, irritable, nervous, food craving, among other symptoms such as breakout, bloating, constipation, or diarrhoea. Nevertheless, not all the factors are felt by everyone and need more diagnoses.”Dr Rhythm Bhalla, senior consultant in obstetrics and gynaecology at Cocoon Hospital, Chandigarh, similarly notes that symptoms can begin before the next period arrives.“The physical effects of menstrual cycle on women may start long before the upcoming period. Variations in levels of oestrogen and progesterone affect moods, sleep, eating and energy levels. However, there is no standard experience in this regard since some women feel better before ovulation whereas some start experiencing fatigue, poor sleep, cravings and irritability prior to the onset of the period. Women may start experiencing acne and bloating, while digestive problems may turn into constipation or diarrhoea before the period starts. There may be minor symptoms but serious problems should not be overlooked.”Despite menstruation being a regular part of life for millions of women, understanding of the complete menstrual cycle remains uneven.Many learn the basics at school or at home but receive little information about ovulation, hormonal fluctuations and the physical and emotional changes that can occur throughout the menstrual cycle.When asked whether they knew that hormonal changes continue throughout the month, even when they are not bleeding, the responses revealed varying levels of awareness.Vijaya said, “Yes. The whole cycle is in process and goes beyond just shedding blood. There is constant hormonal fluctuations which ultimately affects the energy and motivation throughout the lifetime.”Prisha Patnaik responded, “Yes, I think 4 phases?” while Shivanghi said, “I have a broad idea, like the luteal, follicular phases and all. Not really informed about the details.”Their responses point to a distinction between knowing that the menstrual cycle involves hormonal changes and understanding how these changes unfold across its different phases.For many, school provides only the basics, leaving them to turn to family members, friends or online resources for more information. Others have to seek answers on their own.Vijaya said, “I didn't learn about periods at home, it was only until I got them did I have the conversation. In school it was only what textbook had to offer, they didn't even teach about pads etc.”Priyanka said, “I learnt the basics at school, but very little about hormonal changes and their impact on our bodies. One common misconception I've encountered is that periods are just about bleeding, when they actually affect our physical and emotional well-being throughout the month.”Sneha said, “I don’t have much to say about how periods were discussed at school. I got most of my information at home and from Google, which I explored out of curiosity.”These experiences underline the need for menstrual-health education that goes beyond explaining bleeding.Girls and boys need age-appropriate information about the menstrual cycle, reproductive health, common symptoms and when medical attention may be necessary.The gap is not just in what women are taught, but also in how menstruation is discussed. For Sasha, her first lessons about periods at school offered little insight into the subject.Years later, she encountered another misconception in the workplace, where her mood was sometimes attributed to menstruation.“When I worked in an all-boys work desk, I was often asked if I was on periods if I was not in a cheerful mood. Bad mood can be a product of multiple things, not just periods,” she added.In many parts of India, menstruation remains a subject surrounded by stigma and silence. Some women continue to face restrictions on entering kitchens, touching utensils, participating in religious activities or discussing periods openly.Pari (name changed), from Assam, describes the restrictions followed in her household."On the three days of my period, I sit and sleep on the floor. I eat on a separate plate as I am not allowed to enter the kitchen or touch any utensil or other furniture. I do not touch any male member be it my father, brother or husband. These customs have been followed for a very long time in my household and me, my mother and sister have applied the same in our lives."Her account reflects how cultural practices can shape women's experiences of menstruation beyond the physical symptoms themselves.Yash Sonkar points to the gaps in menstrual-health education, saying, “Menstruation isn’t even properly explained in our school curriculum… teachers skip the chapters at times.”For Trisha, the problem goes beyond inadequate education to the stigma surrounding menstruation. One of the most persistent misconceptions she has encountered, she says, is that periods make women “impure”.Vijaya's experience reflects how deeply such beliefs can become embedded in everyday life. “As for misconceptions, it's hard to think of one that I might not have been forced on. Days on which I can cut my nails, touching the pickle, touching gods or even mentioning it in front of a male entity,” she says, recalling the restrictions associated with menstruation.These beliefs can persist through seemingly ordinary practices, from discouraging women from entering places of worship to treating menstruation as something that must be kept out of sight.Even the habit of wrapping sanitary napkins discreetly or avoiding conversations about periods can reinforce the idea that menstruation is something to hide rather than a normal biological process.The menstrual cycle is regulated by a complex interaction between the brain, the ovaries and the uterus. Several factors can interfere with this process, affecting ovulation, the timing of periods and the amount of bleeding.Dr Susawat explains that stress can affect the hormones involved in ovulation, potentially delaying periods or causing them to be missed. Thyroid disorders can influence cycle length and bleeding patterns, while PCOS may interfere with regular ovulation and lead to irregular or absent periods.Age is another factor. Cycles may be irregular during the years after menstruation first begins and may change again during perimenopause, the transition towards menopause. Hormonal contraception can also alter bleeding patterns, depending on the method used.Dr Bhalla said that the cycle depends on several systems working together. “Periods are the result of interaction between the brain, the ovaries and the uterus; there are many things that might interfere in this interaction. Stress, combined with big changes in weight or poor eating habits, may lead to ovulation delay,” Bhalla said.“Thyroid issues may cause changes in bleeding amount and frequency. In PCOS, ovulation may be less frequent and make periods irregular. The menstrual problems can occur during the period of adolescence before the beginning of menopause. As hormonal contraceptives have an impact on the level of reproductive hormones and uterine lining in some form, so the bleeding can be less, spotting or absence of periods can occur,” she added.This means that a change in the menstrual cycle does not necessarily indicate a serious health problem, but persistent changes should not be ignored.A healthcare professional may consider factors such as stress, medication, pregnancy, thyroid function and PCOS when assessing irregular periods.Although changes in mood, energy and physical comfort may occur throughout the menstrual cycle, not every symptom should be attributed to hormones.According to Dr Susawat, excessive bleeding between periods, bleeding after sexual intercourse, persistent pelvic pain or pain during intercourse should be evaluated. Unusual vaginal discharge accompanied by an odour, irritation or fever also warrants medical attention.She highlights that women should seek an assessment if their menstrual pattern changes significantly or if they miss periods for three months. If pregnancy is possible, a missed period may be a reason to take a pregnancy test.Dr Bhalla similarly advises that frequent bleeding between cycles, bleeding after intercourse, persistent pelvic pain and unusual discharge accompanied by itching, a bad odour or fever should not be ignored.“This can be explained through the normal process of a woman. Abnormal bleeding that occurs frequently in between cycles, or bleeding following sexual intercourse, or constant pain in the pelvis area or during sexual intercourse should be dealt with appropriately. Unusual vaginal discharge accompanied by signs such as itching, bad odor and fever should be attended to. Irregular periods which result in absence of menstruation for over three months should also be considered and an examination carried out. This should be done as early as possible if pregnancy is one of the probable causes. Severe pelvic pain in addition to bleeding, missing periods and fainting should be handled as a matter of urgency. Excessive vaginal bleeding accompanied by weakness, dizziness and difficulty breathing should also be handled urgently,” she said.Other warning signs include bleeding that lasts longer than seven days, very heavy bleeding, severe or worsening menstrual pain and symptoms that interfere with work, studies or daily activities.Heavy bleeding can lead to iron deficiency anaemia, particularly when it occurs repeatedly. Severe menstrual pain may also be associated with conditions such as endometriosis or adenomyosis, while irregular cycles may warrant assessment for PCOS, thyroid disorders or other underlying causes.Severe pelvic pain accompanied by a missed period, bleeding or faintness requires urgent medical assessment, particularly when pregnancy is possible.The key is to recognise the difference between a symptom that occurs occasionally and one that is persistent, severe or unusual for the individual.The World Health Organisation (WHO) recognises menstrual health as more than a matter of managing bleeding. It includes access to accurate information, affordable menstrual products, safe sanitation facilities, appropriate healthcare and the ability to participate in everyday life without stigma.The WHO has also highlighted the limited availability of high-quality scientific research on menstruation. Better research and education can help improve care, support health policies and challenge myths surrounding the menstrual cycle.The organisation estimates that around 500 million people who menstruate worldwide lack access to the full range of menstrual-health materials, facilities and services. It has also cited emerging national data indicating that around 39% of schools provide menstrual-health education.These gaps matter because a lack of information can prevent women from recognising symptoms that require medical attention. It can also make it harder for them to discuss menstrual difficulties without embarrassment or fear of being dismissed.The menstrual cycle is a continuous process shaped by hormones, reproductive health, age and individual circumstances.While some women experience significant physical and emotional changes throughout the month, others notice little variation beyond menstruation.Understanding these differences can help women recognise their own patterns, question symptoms that disrupt daily life and seek medical advice when necessary.Better menstrual-health education can also challenge misconceptions and make conversations about periods less uncomfortable.Men, too, have a role to play. When partners understand the physical and emotional changes women may experience throughout the cycle, they can offer greater empathy, support and understanding instead of dismissing symptoms or attributing every change in mood to menstruation.
Article Summary: The days leading up to a period can be just as challenging as the bleeding itself. Menstruation is the shedding of the uterine lining through the vagina when pregnancy has not occurred. The bleeding contains blood and tissue from the lining of the uterus, also called the endometrium.

Article Title: 'Interference in internal affairs': India rebukes UN human rights body over Delhi protest crackdown
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: India on Sunday rejected the UN human rights body's concerns over the security crackdown ahead of the Cockroach Janta Party's (CJP) proposed protest in Delhi, calling them “unwarranted” and an “unacceptable interference” in the country's internal affairs.In a statement, the ministry of external affairs said "India is the world’s largest democracy, where the right to peaceful assembly is guaranteed by our Constitution and safeguarded by robust institutions, an independent judiciary and a free media."“As in every democracy, Indian citizens exercise this right subject to the maintenance of public order and safety. Our law enforcement authorities act strictly in accordance with the law, and our courts remain available to all for the redressal of any grievances,” the ministry said.The MEA also accused the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) of being selective in its public statements, alleging that it had remained silent on violent responses to protests in neighbouring countries and law enforcement actions closer to its own headquarters.“Such double standards only erode the credibility of its standing and contribute to the loss of faith in multilateralism,” the statement said.The response came a day after the UN human rights chief expressed concern over reports of mass detentions of demonstrators, protest leaders, civil society members, lawyers and journalists before and during large-scale demonstrations in Delhi.“We call on the authorities to ensure that the right to peaceful assembly is fully respected and fulfilled. Restrictions on peaceful protests must meet strict tests of necessity and proportionality,” the high commissioner for human rights said.The proposed CJP demonstration sought the removal of CEC Gyanesh Kumar over the SIR of electoral rolls. The protest was met with a heavy security deployment and crackdown, and several political leaders and demonstrators were detained.
Article Summary: India rejects the UN human rights body's concerns over the security crackdown ahead of the Cockroach Janta Party's (CJP) proposed protest in Delhi. The MEA also accused the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) of being selective in its public statements.

Article Title: ‘Thanks for teaching youngsters’: Tharoor takes dig at PM Modi, shares 2015 tweet
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: Congress leader Shashi Tharoor late Saturday took a dig at Prime Minister Narendra Modi by sharing his 2015 tweet about the Emergency. Tharoor drew a parallel with the current situation in Delhi, where police cracked down on protesters demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.“Thanks for teaching today’s youngsters many of the same lessons, Modiji!” Tharoor wrote on X while sharing Modi’s post dated June 25, 2015. In the old tweet, Modi had said, “Personally, the Emergency brings back many memories. As youngsters, we learnt a lot during the anti-Emergency movement.”Tharoor’s jibe came on a day of heightened security, mass detentions and a political showdown in the national capital, where a protest organised by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) was met with a heavy police deployment. 7,000 people were detained (and later released), including several Opposition leaders, while 45 Metro stations were closed till 10pm amid extensive security arrangements.Earlier in the day, Tharoor had criticised the government over the restrictions, describing the situation as a “war-like deployment” and saying that “our GenZ deserves better than an undeclared Emer-GenZ”.The Thiruvananthapuram MP said he had returned to Delhi after 2 am and had rarely witnessed anything like the security measures in place across the capital.He cited checkpoints, concrete barricades, spike strips, the deployment of 22,000 police and paramilitary personnel, cancelled train services and reports of young people being detained.Questioning the suspension of internet services in the heart of the national capital and restrictions on access to Jantar Mantar, Tharoor said the government should answer questions about the integrity of elections rather than prevent citizens from raising them.“The government should provide answers, not lathis; expression, not repression,” he said, adding that barricades would do nothing to restore public faith in the Election Commission.The CJP protest had triggered a wider political confrontation, with Opposition leaders accusing the government of suppressing democratic dissent, while the BJP accused protest organisers of attempting to destabilise the country.Delhi Police sources told ANI that all detainees had been released from detention centres except CJP leaders, for whom due legal process would be followed. The Supreme Court is scheduled to hear a contempt petition on Sunday over allegations that the closure of Metro stations violated its October 9 order.
Article Summary: Tharoor’s jibe came on a day of heightened security, mass detentions and a political showdown in the national capital. In the old tweet, Modi had said, “Personally, the Emergency brings back many memories. As youngsters, we learnt a lot during the anti-Emergency movement.”

Article Title: Suvendu eyes Bengal sweep: Can Mamata, Congress unite to challenge BJP?
Article Text:
West Bengal CM Suvendu Adhikari

Bypolls have usually favoured the ruling party

Suvendu's promise

Why BJP's victories still matter

Allegations of electoral excesses

BJP supporters in Rejinagar

What's next for the Opposition?

Mamata Banerjee's political journey before becoming CM

Municipal elections: The next big battle

Road to 2029

Former Bengal CM Mamata Banerjee detained during protest in New Delhi

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

"We are set to win 42 out of 42 in the 2029 Lok Sabha election." West Bengal CM Suvendu Adhikari had made this grandiose claim even before the Nandigram and Rejinagar bypoll results. A visibly buoyant Adhikari reiterated the target after his party swept both seats. Victories in both constituencies were expected, yet the margins, particularly in Rejinagar, where roughly 70% of voters are Muslim, came as a revelation. With the all-important Kolkata and Howrah municipal polls likely to be held in late November, there is a perception that the BJP may win handsomely. It is up to the Opposition to put up a spirited fight.What may give the Opposition some solace is the fact that bypolls, at least over the last decade or so, have followed an extremely predictable pattern in Bengal. Between the 2021 and 2026 Assembly elections, Trinamool won 20 of the 21 Assembly bypolls held in the state. Its dominance was particularly striking in 2024, when it swept all 12 by-elections, including four seats previously held by BJP legislators.In July 2024, Trinamool wrested Raiganj, Ranaghat Dakshin and Bagdah from the BJP despite the latter's electoral strength in these areas during the Lok Sabha election just weeks earlier.In November, TMC captured Madarihat, which the BJP had held since 2016. Even in June 2025, less than a year before its Assembly rout, Trinamool retained Kaliganj by more than 50,000 votes.There have been exceptions to the incumbent's advantage. In 2023, Congress , supported by the Left, defeated the ruling TMC in Sagardighi by nearly 23,000 votes. However, the MLA concerned, Bayron Biswas, soon joined TMC.In Nandigram, BJP's Hasi Rani Rath defeated Congress candidate Milan Pradhan, who had Mamata's support, by 1,22,753 votes. In Rejinagar, BJP's Shankharavh Sarkar defeated Aam Janata Unnayan Party candidate Golam Nabi Azad, son of party founder Humayun Kabir, by more than 75,000 votes.In both constituencies, BJP polled more votes than all its opponents combined. Rejinagar witnessed notable outreach from the CM, with Suvendu even saying that Muslims did not need to chant "Jai Shri Ram". He also urged them to turn over a new leaf and extend a hand of friendship to the new government.Following the result, Adhikari attributed BJP's success partly to support from beneficiaries of the Annapurna welfare scheme, under which eligible women receive ₹3,000 per month. Whether the BJP can really secure a share of the Muslim vote in elections with bigger stakes remains to be seen. But if it does, Suvendu's dream of a clean sweep in the Lok Sabha election may well look more realistic.The Opposition, though, has refused to grant legitimacy to the Assembly bypolls, citing alleged malpractices by the ruling machinery. Bengal Congress president Subhankar Sarkar demanded fresh elections in both constituencies, alleging booth capturing, intimidation, bogus voting and the forcible removal of polling agents. AJUP, which had won the seat previously, alleged that its candidate received zero votes in 33 booths and just one vote in another 19 booths. Mamata's TMC faction made similar allegations of rigging, while the rival Trinamool faction and the Left also complained about polling agents being prevented from functioning.In Nandigram, Congress candidate Milan Pradhan alleged that party agents had been driven out of booths and voters prevented from voting. His earlier arrest in connection with an old case related to the Nandigram land movement had already prompted allegations of political harassment.BJP rejected the rigging allegations, maintaining that polling was peaceful. The Election Commission described voting as largely peaceful despite receiving complaints. One widely circulated claim that BJP had received more votes than the number of registered voters at a Rejinagar booth was subsequently rebutted by election officials, who said the original electorate figure was incorrect.Such allegations are not new to Bengal's electoral politics, one of the reasons why the opposition have frequently asked for central forces to conduct polls. The 2018 panchayat elections witnessed widespread reports of violence and intimidation. More than a third of the seats were won uncontested, overwhelmingly by Trinamool, amid allegations that opposition candidates had been prevented from filing nominations. A year later, the BJP increased its Lok Sabha tally in Bengal from two seats in 2014 to 18 in 2019.Political observers have linked that breakthrough partly to resentment over the conduct of the panchayat polls. Very recently, Abhishek Banerjee’s Diamond Harbour model of winning by record margin of votes had also come under scrutiny. For BJP though, barely a few months into power, the chances of pushback to any alleged excesses remain relatively modest.The INDIA bloc has upped the ante in the capital, demanding the resignation of CEC Gyanesh Kumar over alleged vote manipulation during the SIR process. Leaders such as Rahul Gandhi, Mamata Banerjee and even those from the Left have been sharing the stage. With a common goal, the confluence is organic. But the state-level dynamics are very different, something that has affected the INDIA alliance for a long time.An INDIA alliance is unlikely to become a reality in Bengal, with Left and TMC cadres rarely seeing eye to eye. An alliance between Mamata's TMC and Congress remains an open question, with state leaders of the grand old party lukewarm about giving space to a leader who did not allow them much room to grow while in power.Mamata came to power in 2011 in alliance with Congress, but the two soon parted ways. Since then, the parties have hardly worked together politically, until this by-election. There have been several overtures from Congress in the past, but these were rebuffed by the then West Bengal CM, who wanted to maximise her political capital. Now that the script has flipped, Congress may not give in so easily.Former state Congress president Pradip Bhattacharya disclosed in September that the state leadership had advised against a proposed bypoll arrangement under which Congress would contest Nandigram and Mamata's Trinamool would fight Rejinagar. Adhir Ranjan Chowdhury's recent invitation to Mamata to return to Congress with her remaining MLAs and MPs came with a condition about leaving behind her political baggage, widely interpreted as a reference to Abhishek Banerjee.Even the Nandigram understanding was not a formal seat-sharing arrangement. Mamata supported Milan Pradhan after her faction's candidate withdrew. In Rejinagar, both parties contested separately. Many Congress leaders believe that it is time to rebuild the party in the state when opposition space is up for grabs. The BJP is still getting to grips with governance, and teething troubles in several areas, including the rollout of government schemes, have made headlines.The organisational crisis within Trinamool adds another dimension. Following the Assembly defeat, the party split into rival factions, prompting the Election Commission to temporarily freeze its original name and symbol. The Mamata-led faction and the Ritabrata Banerjee-led Democratic Trinamool Congress contested under different identities in the bypolls. Neither performed well. In Rejinagar, Mamata's faction received 3,847 votes, while Democratic Trinamool polled 2,044.The Left, meanwhile, continues to face the challenge of translating political visibility into electoral support. Younger leaders such as Satarup Ghosh, Dipshita Dhar and Srijan Bhattacharya have attracted attention, particularly on social media, but the party's electoral recovery remains limited.There were, however, modest improvements in the latest bypolls. In Nandigram, the CPI's Santi Gopal Giri increased his tally from 2,997 votes in May to 5,779. Congress also improved its vote count in both constituencies, although the Nandigram comparison is complicated by Mamata's support for its candidate.The immediate electoral focus now shifts to the Kolkata and Howrah municipal polls, where voting is tentatively expected in late November. The stakes extend far beyond the two Assembly bypolls.In the 2021 Kolkata Municipal Corporation election, Trinamool won 134 of 144 wards, securing more than 72% of the votes. BJP won just three wards and Congress two. Interestingly, the Left Front, with nearly 12% of the vote, finished ahead of BJP in vote share despite winning fewer seatstThe forthcoming election will also be fought on a substantially altered map. Kolkata's wards have increased from 144 to 209, and Howrah's from 50 to 68. For both factions of TMC, this election will be the first major test of who enjoys greater public support. For Mamata Banerjee, south Kolkata remains her pocket borough, and following the humiliating defeat in Bhabanipur, she would be desperate to turn around her fortunes. For Firhad Hakim and others, it will be an opportunity to prove that they can win on their own without Didi's support.Congress and the Left have long been marginal forces in both Kolkata and Howrah, barring a few pockets. The Left appears inclined to contest independently in several areas, although the CPM has encouraged local discussions with Congress. Some Congress district leaders, meanwhile, have argued that the party should contest all 209 Kolkata wards on its own.The decisions are yet to be finalised, leaving Congress with a difficult choice between rebuilding independently, cooperating with the Left and exploring an understanding with Mamata.Nationally, Rahul Gandhi's success in rallying different INDIA bloc parties in the campaign demanding the resignation of the CEC has done his popularity no harm. The bonhomie between Sonia Gandhi and Mamata Banerjee at the recent press conference was there for everyone to see. They have maintained cordial personal relations despite the ebbs and flows in their political exchanges. But the political calculations in Bengal remain very different. Rahul's pointed attacks on Trinamool over corruption during the Assembly campaign had reinforced the Congress's adversarial position in the state. For local Congress workers, a sudden statewide alliance with Mamata would require a significant political adjustment. Didi however, remains in the frontlines in the protest against Election Commission and was detained on Saturday even as Rahul Gandhi skipped the protest and went to Chennai.At the same time, Mamata faces one of the most difficult phases of her political career, while the BJP confronts increasingly coordinated opposition protests at the national level. Hence the political equations could well change. After the municipal elections in Kolkata and Howrah, polls in more than 100 other civic bodies are expected next year, followed by panchayat polls in 2028 and the Lok Sabha election in 2029. Those who have power in the grassroots are likely to have a headstart in the Lok Sabha election.Suvendu has already set his sights on winning all 42 Lok Sabha seats in Bengal. Such a result would have significant implications for the BJP's national parliamentary tally. For Congress, the calculation is therefore not confined to the revival of its Bengal organisation. Its leadership must also consider the wider political ramifications of allowing the BJP a free-run in the state.For the Opposition, national unity over electoral issues is one thing. Building an effective political arrangement in Bengal is quite another. The coming municipal elections will provide the first major opportunity to see whether those differences can be bridged.
Article Summary: West Bengal CM Suvendu Adhikari had made grandiose claim even before the Nandigram and Rejinagar bypoll results. Bypolls, at least over the last decade or so, have followed an extremely predictable pattern in Bengal. Trinamool won 20 of the 21 Assembly bypolls.

Article Title: ‘Grandmother's rites on hold': Abhijeet Dipke's mother claims Delhi Police is lying over giving him the news
Article Text:
Abhijeet Dipke’s mother says family unable to contact him

NEW DELHI: The mother of Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke, Anita Dipke, on Sunday accused Delhi Police of lying about informing her son of his grandmother’s death, saying the family had been unable to contact him and had postponed the last rites until he could return.“We have not been able to contact him...Delhi Police is lying. If he got the news (his grandmother's demise), he would have come immediately...we have put the last rites on hold for him...” Anita Dipke said.Delhi Police had earlier said it informed Dipke about his grandmother’s death while he remained in detention in the national capital ahead of the party’s proposed protest against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.“It is now up to him whether he wants to stay back and continue the protest under detention or fly back for the last rites,” Delhi Police sources told news agency ANI on Saturday.Dipke’s paternal grandmother, Savitribai Shankarrao Dipke, 85, died at her home in Santuk Pimpri village in Maharashtra’s Hingoli district at 11.30 am on Saturday following a prolonged illness, family sources told PTI. She had been unwell for about a month and was previously hospitalised in Hingoli.Her last rites were scheduled for 10 am on Sunday.An Executive Magistrate has ordered the release of CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke, co-convenor Saurav Das and party leader Ashutosh Ranka following their preventive detention by Delhi Police on Saturday.The three were detained after arriving in the national capital from Mumbai to participate in the party’s proposed ‘Jantar Mantar 2.0’ protest, which sought the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.Delhi Police had denied permission for the demonstration, citing public safety, traffic management and law-and-order concerns. Security was subsequently tightened across the capital ahead of the planned protest.
Article Summary: Anita Dipke, mother of CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke says family unable to contact him. Delhi Police had earlier said it informed Dipke about his grandmother’s death while he remained in detention in the national capital. Savitribai Shankarrao Dipke died on Saturday following a prolonged illness.

Article Title: Personality rights: HC asks Amitabh Bachchan to appear if settlement fails
Article Text: NEW DELHI: Delhi HC has asked Amitabh Bachchan to appear in person if a settlement with several defendants in a personality rights case remains incomplete and he still wishes to pursue his claims.Justice Purushaindra K Kaurav passed the direction after the court was informed an amicable settlement had been reached with some defendants through mediation, but could not be formally signed due to logistical issues on Bachchan’s side.The court granted time to the actor to complete formalities and place the formal agreement on record. The next hearing will be on Nov 16.The HC said in the event of a non-settlement or incomplete settlement, Bachchan would have to be personally present if he wished to pursue any of his claims. His presence would enable the court to exercise its powers under provisions of Code of Civil Procedure and Section 168 of BSA, the order underlined. Section 168 empowers a judge to ask any question about any fact s/he considers necessary.
Article Summary: Delhi HC has asked Amitabh Bachchan to appear in person if a settlement with several defendants in a personality rights case remains incomplete. Justice Purushaindra K Kaurav passed the direction after the court was informed an amicable settlement had been reached with some defendants through mediation.

Article Title: CJP leaders' detention: Here’s all that happened on board AI 2428
Article Text:
Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Soon after touching down at Delhi Airport around 10.30 am Saturday with Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) representatives Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka on board, the pilots operating AI 2428 were asked to head to a remote bay instead of a parking stand that is connected to an aerobridge. As directed by air traffic control, the ex-Vistara Airbus A320 (VT-TQL) headed to a bay closer to the international wing of T3 and parked there.Then, sources say, the pilots were informed that a team of security personnel would board the aircraft. A passenger stair car (vehicle with a step ladder) got attached and a team of Delhi Police personnel boarded the aircraft and went to the row where CJP representatives were seated. They asked the three to accompany them as they were being detained.“I have come here to be arrested; arrest me,” Dipke is heard telling the police team in videos shot inside the aircraft. The police personnel are heard responding: “No, this is not an arrest. Please cooperate.” Once the security personnel and the three CJP representatives left the aircraft, the process began for other passengers who had to remain seated for 10-15 minutes to do so.With changed wind direction, aircraft at that time were landing from Dwarka side (this one touched down on IGIA’s fourth runway 11L/29R) and it takes a much longer taxi to reach T3 as they land towards Shivji statue side and then taxi back towards the terminal from taxiway.Air India did not comment on what happened onboard AI 2428. While it is not uncommon for criminals and unruly passengers to be escorted out of aircraft after landing by security agencies, political or social activists getting this treatment is not something that happens frequently.Bay allocation is done by the airport operator, in this case Delhi Interna­tional Airport Ltd. In “special circumstances” like that Saturday, govt agencies can direct the operator to allocate a remote bay to aircraft. That also happens to aircraft for which a bomb threat has been received.Pilots of AI 2428 were asked to proceed to the remote bay after they landed. Air traffic control guides pilots to the bay they have been allocated by asking them to take taxiway routings.“Aviation in general and airports in particular operate in a highly regulated environment. We just get instructions from govt agencies from time to time and have to follow them,” said aviation industry long timers.
Article Summary: Pilots of AI 2428 were asked to proceed to the remote bay after they landed. Air traffic control guides pilots to the bay they have been allocated by asking them to take taxiway routings. Bay allocation is done by the airport operator, in this case Delhi Interna­tional Airport Ltd.

Article Title: Parliament, not streets, will govern country: BJP; govt is rattled, says oppn
Article Text:
BJP says protest a flop; oppn puts united front

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Opposition parties on Saturday lashed out at govt over wide security curbs to foil the Cockroach Janta Party's call for protest at Jantar Mantar but a defiant BJP backed the clampdown, saying Parliament, and not streets, will run the country.BJP president Nitin Nabin alleged two anarchic groups - one of the INDIA bloc and another led by Arvind Kejriwal and his "associate" CJP, were seeking to stoke unrest in the country and were in a battle of one-upmanship over spreading chaos: "They are working in collusion with foreign forces to destabilise India."Congress, which kept away from Saturday's protests, lent its support to the agitating youths and said their "peaceful" stir has left govt rattled and nervous.Leader of the Opposition in Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi said, "Youth of India, I am proud of you. Keep protesting. We are standing with you. I have been fighting Narendra Modi and the RSS for over a decade now. The core characteristic of these people is cowardice.""Narendra Modi, Amit Shah, Mohan Bhagwat, Gyanesh Kumar and Ajit Doval, the villains of this story, are slowly finding the space closing around them. We are closing that space," he added, claiming that govt may further ramp up security measures but protests over the SIR issue will continue.A combative BJP was, however, categorical that CJP, which had "broken" the conditions under which their members were allowed to launch their stir in July, could not have been allowed to "hijack" Jantar Mantar again. "Democracy has prevailed over anarchy. The country will be governed through Parliament, not the streets. The country cannot be run by spreading anarchy on the streets," Ravi Shankar Prasad said.Speaking at the sixth edition of his youth outreach programme, 'Chhatron Ki Goonj' at Chennai's Island Grounds, Rahul said "Mogambo Modi" was destroying India's democracy, referring to the PM. "Mr Modi doesn't understand that the game is over," he added. "I want to tell all the students in Delhi, do not worry. Stand up for everything you believe in and never stop asking questions," Gandhi said, asserting, "We are standing with you. "SP president Akhilesh Yadav said, "Now, the nation will unite in Delhi! We stand with the youthful energy of the nation. If BJP govt thinks it can halt the people through the might of power, this will prove to be an even greater mistake on its part." Article Title: Restrained, detained, contained: Clampdown foils stir, thousands confined to home, nabbed on way
Article Text:
Security arrangements may not see let-up today

NEW DELHI: Unprecedented security arrangements from central Delhi to the borders, phalanxes of 35,000 police and paramilitary personnel and a virtual choke on metro services and trains foiled Cockroach Janta Party's march to Jantar Mantar on Saturday. The city, however, remained on edge, with young protesters being detained on their way to the protest site and bundled into buses and vans, kicking and screaming, through the day.With CJP's Abhijeet Dipke, Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das detained at the airport, the outfit's national organisation in-charge, Ajinkya Shinde, was named to lead the protests. The computer science grad, a former AAP worker, said protests would continue till Gyanesh Kumar resigned as CEC.With top CJP functionaries being kept away from Jantar Mantar, small groups dodged security personnel and staged flash protests at Safdarjung flyover, Dilli Haat and Gurdwara Bangla Sahib complex, among other places.The impromptu gathering near Safdarjung flyover by AISA national president Neha Bora, lawyer Prashant Bhushan, political commentator Yogendra Yadav, and several others caught police off-guard momentarily around 1pm.The protesters were eventually detained.It was obvious since Thursday that the call by CJP, supported by some political outfits, for a protest against the CEC and SIR at Jantar Mantar at 10am on Saturday would be met with stiff resistance. New Delhi was divided into 20 zones, with 1-2 companies of CAPF and Delhi Police deployed at every nook and corner. BSF was also present at the city's borders.Water cannons and tear-gas vehicles were kept ready. Multiple layers of barricades were erected and police personnel closely questioned people heading towards the New Delhi area, particularly in the direction of Jantar Mantar. Police said there were only some isolated incidents of minor confrontations. While three or four personnel, including women, were injured in incidents of stone-pelting and other skirmishes, a DCP fractured his hand, they said.Police claimed they had detained 2,500 people in the city — 600-700 people on stretches leading to Jantar Mantar, and others from different parts of Delhi, including the borders. The police figures were, however, hotly contested, with sources saying around 7,000 people were detained, counting those who were not allowed to leave their homes and were put under preventive detention.CJP’s Ajinkya Shinde, who will lead the protests now, alleged more than 15,000 people, including students, civil society members and political functionaries, had been illegally detained across the country. An undeclared emergency had been imposed in Delhi, he said.Police said apart from the fact that permission had not been given for the protest, prohibitory orders under Section 163 of Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) were in force, making the proposed gathering illegal.Four former chief ministers — Aam Aadmi Party convener Arvind Kejriwal, Trinamool Congress chief Mamata Banerjee, Kerala’s Pinarayi Vijayan, and Manik Sarkar of Tripura — were detained. CPM veteran Brinda Karat, Rajya Sabha MP John Brittas, and TMC functionaries Derek O’Brien and Dola Sen were also detained.Detained protesters were taken in buses to Chhatrasal Stadium, Rajiv Gandhi Stadium, Yamuna Sports Complex and Surajmal Stadium, all designated earlier for this purpose. Around 600 buses, including some from Third Battalion used to transport prisoners, were used to ferry those detained.Around 9pm, police claimed they had released everyone, but refused to respond when asked about Dipke, Ranka and Das. Multiple cases will be registered in connection with violation of prohibitory orders and assault, besides other sections, police said.With CJP sources saying they will continue their protests and Congress and other INDIA bloc parties planning a march in the city Monday, the security paraphernalia is likely to remain in place for the next few days.
Article Summary: CJP's Abhijeet Dipke, Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das detained at the airport. Ajinkya Shinde, CJP's national organisation in-charge, named to lead the protests. Police claim they had detained 2,500 people in the city.
